You want to look at the noise in the model itself.

For instance, in the soil carbon models, respirated carbon,
which is positive constrained, tends to have lognormal measurement
noise (noise is proportional to measurement rather than being
a constant scale additive term).

There's not a huge difference in efficiency between declaring
a positive value and giving it a lognormal distribution and
declaring an unconstrained value, giving it a normal distribution,
and then exp() transforming it to positive.

- Bob

Linus,

Not to be nitpicky but be careful distinguishing 'measurement' noise - which you might attribute to assay error, which will be normally distributed (your $SIGMA) in nonmem. The lognormal distribution of PK parameters is driven mostly by physiology. Given the etas are normally distributed, you generate the lognormal parameter distribution via

TVP*EXP(nP) 

And FYI, for bayesian models, nonmem will use a normal distribution for variance around thetas and an inverse wichtart distribution for omegas, if you want to match that with STAN.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stiff ODEs and population PK models
parts:
Check out this to develop some intuitions:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

What do you tell people now when they ask you to justify an
(inverse) Wishart?

What the inverse Wishart has going for it is that it's the conjugate
prior for covariance matrices in a multivariate normal model. As
such, it can be represented as prior multivariate normal data.

The LKJ prior is like a beta prior in some ways. The
bigger the parameter, the more concentrated the prior is around the
unit correlation matrix. So it lets you directly parameterize
correlation.

Then you can control the scales any way you want to allow for both long
and short-tailed behavior or zero-avoiding behavior (e.g., Cauchy, normal,
lognormal).

In the 2D case this is like putting a beta prior stretched from (0,1)
to (-1, 1) on the correlation rho, and putting an independent
prior on the scales sigma[1] and sigma[2]:

Sigma = sigma[1] * sigma[1] rho * sigma[1] * sigma[2]
rho * sigma[1] * sigma[2] sigma[2] * sigma[2]

You see people do this all the time in the 2D case and the LKJ
prior is just a natural generalization to higher dimensions.

To gain some degree of separation between the scale priors and
the correlation priors, Gelman and Hill hacked something similar
in their regression book by scaling a covariance matrix with an
inverse Wishart prior. It's much easier to get the effect they were
after with a scaled LKJ prior.

- Bob

awesome. Thanks for taking the time to respond. 

To answer your question - people don't ask at this point. Mainly because of the contraints of what NONMEM gives you (basically only inverse wishart unless you want to jump through a lot of hoops).

Also, other than the very small (passionate) minority, the additional hurdles bayesian analysis poses to the status quo of model development makes it so very few people are developing models in that fashion. It's really only under situations where either

a) you a priori know you want to make quantification and handling of uncertainity 'first class'

b) all other options have failed

are people turning to bayesian techniques.

For example, if you look at the ddmore model repository of ~200 models http://repository.ddmore.eu/ as well as my personal interactions with the model bases at Merck, the FDA, and our own group pushing that number to probably 300+ models, I think less than 5% of the models used full bayes, especially for PK models. You see it more when doing like model based meta analysis or some systems biology/PBPK modeling though, and there only metrum and some select individuals seem to make an consistent noise in the space.

Anyway - I don't want to turn this into an exposition, however if you are interested in the why of lack of full bayes (much of which I bet you can guess at) or what stan can (continue) doing to make a dent in that, I'm happy to expand on the state of things.

Thanks again for the pointers!

Devin

You mean in publishing? Because for the most part, Bayesian

I think as people get more sophisticated in thinking about uncertainty,
(a) will be come a priority, and as they want to build more
sophisticated models, (b) is critical. We've come into projects largely

I know i want a 2 compartment model with linear absorption with covariates of weight and gender, but how do I code that and then look at model diagnostics), and from an acceptance perspective - 'matching' up to historical comparisons. Eg, its very easy at this point to say, model development was performed using step-wise covariate modeling using a forward inclusion criteria of p < 0.05 and backwards step of p < 0.001. Here are x, y, z diagnostic plots. You can point to 20 other publications with similar diagnostics and interpretations. For example, the 2 primary plots shown to demonstrate model adequacy is conditional weighted residuals  and observed vs individual predicted concentrations, both shown here: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries

1) Push out some more (simple, but holistic) examples. 

This is going to be the largest hurdle once the ODE implementation settles. For better or worse, the majority of people will want to 'copy-paste' their way through scenarios they are familiar with to wrap their head around. Many companies have model libraries of 100's of models with 'tricks' on how to implement things. 

For example, I'm picking away at an extremely simple example: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries and the associated code for the project: https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes

Such case studies would cover:
- what the data looks like
- model setup with some information
- diagnostic outputs with some minimal interpretation

I know documentation is so low on priorities for the core team, but without some more examples, people such as myself are stuck being unable to directly contribute because it can be difficult to even get off the ground. 2-3 different case-study-based examples would give enough overlapping surface area to provide a feedback loop of being able to generate more community-driven examples off those templates. Similarly, as I mentioned at the beginning, there needs to be at least some guidance in terms of interpretation. This might be comparing a false model to the true model and noting some of the things, or even just a note here or there about what one might look for. 

2) Provide some 'expert opinion' or commentary from Andrew or others that can allay some question to approaches to model selection. Namely companies often waste time debating over covariate selection. Giving a nod to reasonable approach(es) would be a huge boon. This is made more tricky by the current gold standard of stepwise covariate modeling via change in objective function values does not have a clear a bayesian equivalent?.  Metrum, and myself personally, are using a full model approach to essentially select for covariates that can be deemed clinically relevant based on their posterior distribution http://metrumrg.com/assets/pubs/GastonguayPAGE2011.pdf  

2.1) If accomplishing this requires pre/post-processing, providing some tooling around accomplishing this goal. The #1 way via MLE right now is via step-wise modeling, and much of that is due to it being 'good enough' statistically, and dead simple due to it being implemented as little more than a config file + base model structure http://psn.sourceforge.net/pdfdocs/scm_userguide.pdf I think the above full model approach diagnostics are almost completely implemented from a visually in jonah's bayesplot, but could use some additional helpers for continuous covariates (as shown on slide 27 above).

3) Stay the course with Metrum implementing an events system and general ODE implementation details. I imagine there will also need to be some wrappers/templating around other constructs that might not fall under that initial objective (lag time, bioavailability fractions, transit compartments)?

4) longer term (that I hesitate to even pose at this point due to how many more important fundamental constructs need to be implemented first) an additional abstraction layer to give more nonmem style control-file that removes some constructs like explicitly coding to loop through individuals. For example, you can see here how 1 cmt model with analytical solution is defined for a population. https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes/blob/master/models/one_cmt_iv.cpp vs the current stan implementation https://github.com/charlesm93/example-models/blob/feature/issue-70-PKPDexamples-torsten/PKPD/torsten/TwoCptModelPopulation/TwoCptModelPopulation.stan


By and large, it seems people running models in pharma seem to fall under opposite ends of the spectrum: 1) your formally trained statisticians, and 2) (myself included) have background in biological sciences, some math and have been picking up stats on the way, but virtually no formal training, including 'simple' things like digesting proofs. For those of us in camp #2, there is this huge gap between the baby step of here is bayes rule and why its awesome, to 'introductory' texts where the expectation is still at minimum undergrad courses in inference, probability, and general comfort digesting proofs and formula.   An intermediate ground of applied examples could allow people to more directly connect with the domain while also providing pointers to the theory such that they can digest as they become more comfortable. 


Hopefully not too long winded. 


And as a bonus, here, for example, might be an excellent case study:

Which dose should we choose to maximize the benefit/risk profile in a target population, given rich data from a small subset of individuals studied in a previous trial? Let's say we've done a trial and have data for ~100 individuals at 4 escalating dose levels, each with 4-6 samples. To answer this we will need to do the following 

1) Build and evaluate structural and residual error model(s) - is it one cmt/two cmt, and is the residual error additive, exponential, some combination
    - what are the diagnostic plots/calculated values used to compare such models

2) Determine the effect of covariates on model parameters to determine which to retain, as well as to get a feel for which will need to be most closely monitored for potential dose adjustment in later phases (or to kill the drug all together). 
    - how do you address covariate inclusion/exclusion and overall building



3) Simulate from the final model and compare against some criteria (such as % of individuals in a given exposure window). 
    - how to simulate under different designs

3.5) perform sensitivity analysis to determine the impact of being 'wrong' on a given parameter - say the population variability on clearance - what if it was 50% greater, lower, etc. This can be relevant when moving to different subpopulation, eg studied in healthy now going to sick patients with additional comorbidities that may effect drug clearance.


4) bonus: use the above model as a prior to fit some new data.


Hope this helps.

Devin

>
>
> And as a bonus, here, for example, might be an excellent case study:
>
> Which dose should we choose to maximize the benefit/risk profile in a target population, given rich data from a small subset of individuals studied in a previous trial? Let's say we've done a trial and have data for ~100 individuals at 4 escalating dose levels, each with 4-6 samples. To answer this we will need to do the following
>
> 1) Build and evaluate structural and residual error model(s) - is it one cmt/two cmt, and is the residual error additive, exponential, some combination
>     - what are the diagnostic plots/calculated values used to compare such models
>
> 2) Determine the effect of covariates on model parameters to determine which to retain, as well as to get a feel for which will need to be most closely monitored for potential dose adjustment in later phases (or to kill the drug all together).
>     - how do you address covariate inclusion/exclusion and overall building
>
>
>
> 3) Simulate from the final model and compare against some criteria (such as % of individuals in a given exposure window).
>     - how to simulate under different designs
>
> 3.5) perform sensitivity analysis to determine the impact of being 'wrong' on a given parameter - say the population variability on clearance - what if it was 50% greater, lower, etc. This can be relevant when moving to different subpopulation, eg studied in healthy now going to sick patients with additional comorbidities that may effect drug clearance.
>
>
> 4) bonus: use the above model as a prior to fit some new data.
>
>
> Hope this helps.
>
> Devin

It is a great discussion but I just wanted to chime in with my humble needs...
 
I did comparison with stan cmd 2.13.1 between the performance when jacobian of ODE is not supplied and when jacobian is supplied. Sebastian taught me the trick by using dMod and cOde. My ODE is 34 state and quite stiff. I have lot of parameters but just estimate few of them.
 
1. When jacobian is supplied diagnose gives this result. I am curious how to interpret it but it seems there is big difference between finite differences and model. Can somebody explain why?
TEST GRADIENT MODE
 
 Log probability=-17.7607
 
 param idx           value           model     finite diff           error
         0               0        -40.7104        -40.7104   -1.58568e-008
         1          1.1474        -2.88137       -0.280441        -2.60093
         2         5.39363        -6.77934        -8.89517         2.11583
         3         2.07944       -0.829541         1.06564        -1.89518
2. Variational inference breaks after few iterations because cvode error -4. It might be explained that var inference is not designed to handle such errors.
 
3. Although gradient evaluation for the case when jacobian is supplied is much less the total simulation time is pretty much the same. I am still running second simulations but previous results showed that total time is less when jacobian is not supplied. Strange? Can it be attributed to stiffness?
 
4. Even worse is with convergence. While both converge to the similar posterior the case when jacobian is not supplied shows excellent mixing (visual) while when jacobian is supplied it shows autocorrelation. I still didn't run several disperse chains but can it be explained somehow? Maybe stiffness.
 
Data is simulated so my expectation that supplying jacobian makes posterior estimates easy and fast. All files are attached to make example reproducible. Please note that when generating jacobian I just copy ....stan to ...jac.stan to be consistent with namespace.
 
Thanks for any insights,
Linas
